reason: The cited evidence (E1, E2) directly supports the core premises: it reports nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries, links this to reduced cohesion and intergranular cracking, and demonstrates a segregation-engineering strategy using Cr-rich secondary phases. The temperature and deformation conditions are consistent with the cited study, though the hypothesis slightly overgeneralizes by stating the mechanism 'primarily applies' to single-phase fcc HEAs under low-to-moderate temperatures, while the evidence is from one alloy system.
premises: Rapid nanosegregation of Ni, Cr, and Mn to grain boundaries occurs in single-phase fcc HEAs
This nanosegregation reduces grain boundary cohesion
Reduced cohesion promotes intergranular crack initiation and toughness loss
Segregation engineering (e.g., shifting segregation into Cr-rich secondary phases) can suppress harmful nanosegregation
The mechanism applies under quasi-static deformation at room to moderately elevated temperatures
